findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build downloads and executes whatever content is currently served at this URL. A compromised endpoint, DNS/proxy path, or changed script can execute arbitrary commands in the build environment and ship a compromised image; there is no immutable version, checksum, or signature verification.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: The build pipes a redirect-following HTTP response directly into `sh` without a version, checksum, signature, or HTTP-error check. Any change to the endpoint, redirect target, or delivery path executes arbitrary code during image builds; error pages can also be interpreted as shell input.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This executes whatever content is served by a mutable HTTPS URL as the image build user (root by default). A compromised or changed endpoint can inject code into published images without a source-controlled version or integrity check.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures from the build
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline status is the status of `sh`, not `curl`. If curl fails before writing data, `sh` receives empty input and exits successfully, so Docker can produce an image without the intended installation.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the exported helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this wrapper discards it and returns "", which is also the valid value for a present key mapped to an empty string. Callers of this exported API cannot distinguish missing data from stored empty data.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but LoadOrDefault discards that error and returns "". Since a present map entry may also contain "", callers of this exported API cannot distinguish lookup failure from a real empty value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in the public helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported helper discards that error and returns "". A caller cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key whose stored value is the legitimate empty string.

findings.title: Wait for result delivery before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each send is moved into an untracked goroutine, so Run can return with zero results delivered. A caller that treats Run's return as completion may observe incomplete results or close the results channel, causing these goroutines to panic when they later send.

findings.title: Wait for launched sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job send is detached from Run, so Run can return while goroutines are still sending. A caller that treats Run returning as completion and closes results will cause those goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel"; absent a receiver, they can also remain blocked after Run returns.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every result was sent. It now starts send goroutines and returns immediately, so a caller that closes results after Run returns can race with those goroutines and panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also cannot rely on all results being available at return.

findings.title: Apply the supplied tag to the log output
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature now advertises that callers can supply a tag, but the function body still prints only message. Callers cannot produce tagged log records through this API, so the new public contract is unusable.

findings.title: Require admin status and tenant match before deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || grants deletion when either condition is true: any non-admin user can delete records in their tenant, and an admin from one tenant can delete records belonging to every other tenant. The prior policy required both authorization conditions.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant match before deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes a non-admin for any record in their tenant, and authorizes an admin for records in other tenants. The prior predicate required both role authorization and tenant isolation.

findings.title: Restore admin and tenant checks for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: With `||`, a session `{ isAdmin: false, tenantId: record.tenantId }` is authorized to delete the record, bypassing the admin requirement. It also authorizes an admin whose tenant differs from the record. The previous conjunction required both privileges.

findings.title: Preserve invalid settings errors before overwriting storage
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid settings previously threw from parseSettings, so updateFontSize stopped before calling save. The new catch returns defaults; updateFontSize then changes fontSize and saves the replacement JSON, silently overwriting the invalid persisted value and hiding the parse/validation failure.

findings.title: Propagate invalid-settings errors instead of saving defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts JSON and validation failures into valid defaults. updateFontSize then treats that fallback as parsed user settings and calls save, whereas previously the parse error reached updateFontSize and prevented any write. Updating a font size with malformed or incomplete persisted settings therefore silently overwrites them with a default theme and new font size.

findings.title: Preserve invalid settings instead of overwriting them
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch now turns malformed or schema-invalid stored settings into valid defaults. updateFontSize then changes the font size and calls save, so editing font size after a parse failure persists {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>} and destroys the original stored settings. Previously the parse error propagated and prevented that write.

findings.title: Use the requested commit for report artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` remains the commit resolved from `branch`, but `artifacts` are fetched from `build.ref("verified")`. A report for any branch whose commit differs from `verified` therefore contains artifacts that do not belong to the reported source commit.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", `builtFrom` identifies `build.ref(branch)` while `artifacts` are fetched from `build.ref("verified")`. The report therefore associates the selected branch's commit with unrelated artifacts.

findings.title: Read artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom remains build.ref(branch) while artifacts are fetched from build.ref("verified"). The returned report therefore pairs a branch commit with another commit's artifacts.

findings.title: Restore slicing to honor positive limits
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, the function returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed calls it with 20 at src/feed.ts:9, so feeds with more than 20 entries now return more than 20 items.

findings.title: Restore the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, recentEntries now returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20, then writes page.length items into a 20-element array; feeds with more than 20 entries therefore render more than 20 entries.

findings.title: Honor limit when returning recent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, recentEntries now returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9, so feeds with more than 20 entries are returned in full because the loop extends the initially 20-slot array.

findings.title: Count only emitted entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering stale entries removes their rows, but line 22 still passes entries.length to headerLines. For one live and one stale entry, the output declares '# entry-count: 2' while containing one entry row, causing consumers that rely on the count to misread the manifest.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering stale entries changes the number of emitted rows, while the unchanged header is still passed entries.length. A manifest containing one live and one stale entry declares `# entry-count: 2` but contains only one entry row, breaking consumers that use the header to size or validate the manifest.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest entries
findings.whyItBreaks: When any input entry has stale=true, it is removed from the body but headerLines still receives entries.length. The generated # entry-count therefore claims more entries than the manifest contains, breaking consumers that rely on the header to validate or preallocate for the body.

findings.title: Retain the exported legacy-ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported `ids.FormatLegacyID` is a source-incompatible public API change. Any downstream consumer that still formats persisted or interoperating legacy IDs will fail to compile when upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy-ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported Go API. Removing it makes every downstream package that imports ids and calls FormatLegacyID fail to compile on upgrade; the diff provides no replacement or deprecation path.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting exported ids.FormatLegacyID is a source-compatible API break: any downstream package still formatting persisted or legacy identifiers with this function will fail to compile when upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: This replacement removes the exported shippingQuote(order) function. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile on upgrade; quoteShipping is exported from a different module and is not a drop-in import-path-compatible replacement.

score.error: critic produced no summary or checked list (likely malformed output)

findings.title: Preserve Order as an augmentable interface
findings.whyItBreaks: Order was a public interface and could be extended by downstream module augmentation. Replacing it with a type alias makes an existing `declare module ".../orders" { interface Order { ... } }` consumer fail with a duplicate identifier error on upgrade.

findings.title: Handle malformed stored hashes as authentication failures
findings.whyItBreaks: hmac.compare_digest raises TypeError when stored_hash is None, bytes, or a non-ASCII string. guard() does not catch it, so malformed persisted token data produces an exception instead of its prior 401 response.

findings.title: Return the transformed input instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to execute(input) now fails with "always fails"; callers cannot receive the string result promised by the exported function signature, regressing the prior uppercase transformation.

findings.title: Restore execute's declared string result
findings.whyItBreaks: The public function is declared to return a string, but every invocation now throws before producing a result; existing behavior transformed input to uppercase.

findings.title: Restore execute's result instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute(input) API now throws "always fails", so no caller can obtain the previously supported uppercase string result.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only" at line 25. The new predicate returns false first, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 and the read-only branch is unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the active viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, an active viewer below the attempt limit reached handle() and returned "read-only". This new predicate rejects that same valid request before handle() can apply its viewer-specific behavior, making the read-only branch at line 25 unreachable.

findings.title: Keep eligible viewers on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For { status: "active", role: "viewer", attempts: 0 }, the new role guard makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24. Before this change, the same request passed eligibility and returned "read-only" at the viewer-specific branch.

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: Adding payment === "paid" to canProceed makes saveDraft return "blocked" for { state: "draft", payment: "missing" }. Payment legitimately governs submitting an order, but it does not govern persisting a draft; users can no longer save an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: Adding `payment === "paid"` to the shared predicate changes `saveDraft({ state: "draft", payment: "missing" })` from "saved" to "blocked". Payment is a prerequisite for submitting an order, but not for persisting an unfinished draft.

findings.title: Keep draft saves independent of payment status
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is shared by submitOrder and saveDraft. For { state: "draft", payment: "missing" }, the new payment guard returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" even though an unpaid draft must remain saveable.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, `Snapshot.commit` identifies that channel's head while `Snapshot.files` is read from stable. Consumers receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and can publish or inspect the wrong revision's files.

findings.title: Keep snapshot files aligned with its reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any requested channel whose head differs from stable, `commit` is the requested channel's head but `files` are read from stable. Consumers therefore receive a self-inconsistent snapshot and can publish or inspect stable content while attributing it to the requested channel.

findings.title: Read files from the returned commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from `stable`, the snapshot returns `commit` and `channel` for that channel but `files` from `stable`. Consumers retrieving a snapshot for (for example) `main` will receive a self-inconsistent snapshot and may publish or display the wrong file set.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still always returns 10 items because the implementation continues to use the fixed `max_count = 10`. Callers cannot obtain the newly advertised capped result.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=10)` promises callers control over the result limit, but the implementation still assigns `max_count = 10`; e.g. `build("x", 2)` returns 10 values.

findings.title: Honor the requested limit
findings.whyItBreaks: build(prefix, limit=10) promises a caller-controlled limit, but the implementation still always iterates max_count = 10. For example, build("item", 2) returns ten items rather than two.

findings.title: Validate that parsed integers are positive
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int(-1) returns -1 and parse_positive_int("0") returns 0. The exported name promises a positive result, while charge() then produces negative or zero cents.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int(-1) and parse_positive_int(0) return successfully, so charge can produce negative or zero charges despite its validator's positive-integer contract.

findings.title: Validate that parsed amounts are positive
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int(-1)` returns `-1` despite its public name promising a positive integer. `charge` trusts that promise without further validation, so `charge(-1)` returns `-100`, which can create a negative charge rather than reject an invalid amount.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame instead of mutating it
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function made a copy and returned it, leaving df unchanged. It now writes directly to df, so any caller that reuses the input after applying a mapping observes overwritten values rather than the original data.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation copied df before applying the mapping. The changed assignment mutates the caller-owned DataFrame, so callers that retain df expecting the returned transformed copy now silently lose the original values.

findings.title: Reject or normalize negative values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1`, despite its public name promising a positive result. Its caller therefore produces a negative charge (`-100`) rather than rejecting or safely defaulting invalid negative input.

findings.title: Reject negative values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1`, despite the public name promising a positive result. Its caller consequently produces a negative charge (`-100`), and external callers are invited to rely on a contract the function does not enforce.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-value contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int("-5") returns -5 because the body accepts every parseable i64. Its in-repo caller therefore returns a negative charge (-500), contradicting the public positive-int contract.

findings.title: Avoid moving `items` before calculating its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns the owned `Vec<String>`; because its result is discarded, `items` is moved and dropped. The subsequent `items.len()` is therefore an invalid borrow of a moved value (E0382), preventing the crate from compiling.

findings.title: Avoid moving `items` before computing its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` consumes the `Vec<String>`; the subsequent `items.len()` borrows a moved value and Rust rejects the crate with E0382.

findings.title: Avoid moving items into dbg!
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items);` evaluates and consumes the `Vec<String>`; the following `items.len()` borrows a moved value, causing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Compute paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to a revision other than latest, changedPaths is computed from latest while fromRevision remains the pinned revision. Consumers replaying those paths on fromRevision, as the public Changeset contract requires, receive a changeset for the wrong base and can miss or apply the wrong file changes.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the declared base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` resolves to a revision other than `latest`, `changedPaths` is calculated from `latest` but `fromRevision` remains the pinned revision. Consumers replaying these paths on `fromRevision`, as the public `Changeset` contract requires, receive a changeset for the wrong base revision.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the declared base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` remains the revision resolved from `pinnedTag`, but `changedPaths` now comes from the separately resolved `latest` revision. Consumers replay the paths on `fromRevision` per the exported `Changeset` contract, so when the tags differ they receive a path set for the wrong base revision.

findings.title: Update consumers before renaming email
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`; upgraded databases will reject that query with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users no longer has an email column, but src/query.sql still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any execution after upgrading will fail with an unknown-column error.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`, causing a runtime SQL column-not-found error for that query.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing API key
findings.whyItBreaks: The bk_live_ credential is now stored in version control and returned by every makeClient() call. Anyone with repository access can use it, and all environments are forced to share this production credential instead of their configured BILLING_API_KEY.

findings.title: Restore environment-backed billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: This commits a live-formatted billing key into repository history and makes every deployment use that credential, regardless of its configured BILLING_API_KEY. It also changes missing configuration from an explicit error into an indistinguishable usable-looking client.

findings.title: Remove the hard-coded live billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: A live API key is committed to source control and returned to every caller. Anyone with repository access can extract and use it against the production billing endpoint, and rotating the credential now requires a code deployment.

findings.title: Restore the admin authorization check
findings.whyItBreaks: For an archived project, user.isAdmin=true now returns "forbidden", while user.isAdmin=false falls through to db.delete(project.id). This reverses the prior authorization rule and lets non-admin users purge projects.

findings.title: Restore admin authorization before purging
findings.whyItBreaks: `user.isAdmin=true` now returns `forbidden`, while `user.isAdmin=false` with an archived project reaches `db.delete`. This reverses the prior authorization policy and permits unauthorized deletion.

findings.title: Restore the admin authorization check for project purges
findings.whyItBreaks: For an archived project, user.isAdmin=false now falls through and deletes the project, while user.isAdmin=true returns "forbidden". This reverses the prior authorization rule and permits destructive deletion by non-admin users.

findings.title: Preserve defaults when configuration is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (line 7). Previously startup replaced that value with default workers=1; it now subscripts None, raising TypeError instead of starting with the documented prior default behavior.

findings.title: Restore the missing-config fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path, and startup now immediately evaluates settings["workers"], raising TypeError instead of preserving the prior default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: When the settings path does not exist, load_settings returns None (lines 6-7). startup now subscripts that None value, raising TypeError instead of preserving the prior successful default of one worker.

findings.title: Return submission failures from Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error and returns nil. Callers of this exported API cannot distinguish a declined/failed charge from a completed one and may record it as paid.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge only logs it and returns nil. Its exported error-returning API therefore forces callers to conflate a declined/failed charge with a successful charge, allowing downstream code to mark an unpaid charge as complete.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When gw.Submit fails, Charge logs the error and returns nil at line 19. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a rejected or failed charge from a successful one and may record or report it as paid.

findings.title: Keep tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches setting `name`, a request for the same `name` by tenant B hits `settings:name` and returns tenant A's cached value without calling `store.fetch(tenantB, name)`. This regresses tenant isolation and can expose or apply the wrong tenant's configuration.

findings.title: Include the tenant in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor('tenant-a', 'theme', store) caches tenant-a's value under settings:theme. A later request for ('tenant-b', 'theme') hits that same entry at line 13 and returns tenant-a's setting without calling the tenant-b store.

findings.title: Preserve the exported invalidate function's two-argument API
findings.whyItBreaks: invalidate is exported, so existing TypeScript consumers calling invalidate(tenantId, name) will fail to compile after upgrading. With the required tenant-qualified cache key, invalidation must also remain tenant-specific.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still fetches values per tenant, but its cache key is now only settings:<name>. After tenant A reads a setting, tenant B reading the same name receives tenant A's cached value without calling store.fetch, leaking or misapplying tenant-specific configuration.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two callers can both read remaining=1 before either await resumes. Both save 0, both return true, and two units are granted while local stock ends at 0. The former synchronous method could not interleave this way.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields after reading stock but before updating it. With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls both read 1, both save remaining=0, both set local stock to 0, and both return true. This reports two successful reservations for one item.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: `await this.store.save(...)` yields after reading stock but before decrementing it. Two concurrent calls with one unit both read `remaining === 1`, both save zero, then both return true, so one unit is successfully reserved twice.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, and schedulePoll was updated accordingly, but retry() still multiplies its result by 1,000. The first failed retry consequently sleeps 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms; capped retries sleep 30,000,000 ms instead of 30,000 ms.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff directly
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds (attempt 0 returns 1,000 and caps at 30,000), and polling was updated accordingly. retry() still multiplies its result by 1,000 at src/jobs/retry.ts:12, so a first failed attempt waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) instead of 1s; capped retries wait over 8 hours instead of 30s.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still passes backoff(a) * 1000 to sleep. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) instead of 1 second; the capped delay becomes 30 minutes instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Return close failures from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. A close can report a final write/flush failure, but Save now returns nil after a successful bufio flush, forcing callers of this exported API to treat a failed save as successful.

findings.title: Propagate the final close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close return value is discarded. If Flush succeeds but Close fails, Save returns nil even though the final file write/finalization failed; callers cannot distinguish that failure from a completed save.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred `f.Close()` return value is ignored. Previously, after a successful flush, `Save` returned `f.Close()`'s error; now it reports success when close fails. As exported API, this forces callers to conflate a failed final file operation with a successful save.

findings.title: Include each page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is an exclusive bound, but `range(start, end - 1)` stops one position early. `render_page` and `summarize` therefore omit the last row of every page; with `page_size=1`, all rendered pages are empty.

findings.title: Include the page end row in page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds helper returns a half-open end, but range(start, end - 1) excludes the final valid position. A two-row page returns only its first row; a one-row page returns none. render_page and summarize therefore silently omit every page's last row.

findings.title: Include the page end index when collecting rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The documented half-open bounds are [start, end), but range(start, end - 1) stops one index early. A one-row page returns [], and every other non-empty page loses its last row; render_page and summarize therefore produce incomplete output.

findings.title: Return cache entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: For a normal positive ttlMs, a newly stored entry has age 0 and is deleted as a miss; once its age exceeds ttlMs, the stale value is returned indefinitely. This reverses the TtlCache contract.

findings.title: Remove every completed job when pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the next job into the current index, then forEach advances past it. For `[done, done]`, the first splice removes index 0 and the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore the non-expired cache-entry condition
findings.whyItBreaks: A freshly stored entry has elapsed time near 0, so it fails `elapsed > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, an expired entry satisfies the condition and is returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice the array while iterating with forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts the next item into the current index, but `forEach` advances to the next index; therefore consecutive completed jobs are skipped (for example, `[done, done]` leaves one job). This also changes the prior non-mutating filter behavior by altering the caller's array.

findings.title: Restore the non-expired TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time near zero, so `elapsed > ttlMs` is false and get() deletes it and returns null. Conversely, entries older than the TTL are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Do not splice while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the following index. For `[done, done]`, only the first job is removed and one completed job remains.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before deriving the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.sort()` compares scores as strings. With players ordered as scores `[2, 100, 11]` and `n=1`, this ranks scores as `[2, 11, 100]`, sets the cutoff to `2`, and returns the first input player (score `2`) instead of score `100`. `formatBoard` therefore displays an incorrect leader.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending sort
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() without a comparator sorts numbers as strings. With players ordered as score 9 then 100 and n=1, rankScores returns [9, 100], setting the cutoff to 9; topPlayers then returns the first input player (score 9) instead of the score-100 player.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores [100, 20, 3], reversing that result yields [3, 20, 100], so topPlayers(..., 1) sets a cutoff of 3 and returns the first input player rather than the player with score 100.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing hmac.compare_digest with == makes comparison time depend on matching-prefix length. A remote caller can use response timing to incrementally recover a valid webhook signature and reach processor(payload).

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` leaks how much of the attacker-controlled signature matches the expected HMAC through comparison timing. The prior `hmac.compare_digest` avoided this; an attacker able to make repeated webhook requests can use timing observations to forge a valid signature and reach `processor(payload)`.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Plain string equality short-circuits on the first mismatched character. An attacker able to measure webhook response times can probe matching HMAC prefixes and eventually forge a signature, bypassing the 401 guard in handle().

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits and commits immediately after `_record_ledger`. If either subsequent balance UPDATE fails, the ledger records a completed transfer while one or both account balances are unchanged; if the second UPDATE fails, the debit can persist without the credit.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance writes in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after the ledger insert. If either subsequent balance update fails, the ledger entry remains committed; if the credit update fails after the debit succeeds, funds are removed from the source without being credited to the destination.

findings.title: Keep balance updates in the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert is committed when the transaction context exits, before `_apply_balances` runs. If either balance update then fails, the transfer leaves a durable ledger entry with one or both account balances unchanged, whereas the prior implementation rolled all three writes back together.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing-day key
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used UTC getters. The new local-time getters produce a different key on hosts outside UTC; for example, with TZ=America/Los_Angeles, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31. This also makes sameBillingDay classify dates according to deployment timezone rather than the established UTC billing boundary.

findings.title: Keep billing-day boundaries in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces the established UTC date calculation with local-time getters. The same instant now produces different billing keys depending on the process timezone; e.g. 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 in a UTC-05 runtime. sameBillingDay consequently can classify UTC dates incorrectly near midnight.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing-day key
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate. The new local-time getters classify the same instant differently on hosts outside UTC; for example, an instant at 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes billing day 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles. This changes billing grouping and sameBillingDay results by deployment timezone.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After `readProfile("tenant-a", "alice", fetchProfile)` caches its result, `readProfile("tenant-b", "alice", fetchProfile)` uses the same `"alice"` key and returns tenant-a's Profile at line 16 without calling the tenant-b fetcher. This crosses a tenant boundary and exposes incorrect profile data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After a request for tenant A/account X is cached, a request for tenant B/account X uses the same key and returns tenant A's Profile without calling fetchProfile. The Profile contract includes tenant, so this returns incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After a profile for account `A` is cached for tenant `T1`, a request for `(T2, A)` returns T1's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile. The Profile contains tenant-specific data, so this returns the wrong tenant's profile and can disclose cross-tenant information.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: `load` is exported and previously threw for an absent key; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from an explicitly stored empty value. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking data rather than reporting that any requested key was missing.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a key intentionally stored with an empty value. loadAll consequently returns a seemingly valid array containing "" instead of propagating the missing-key failure.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors instead of returning an empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `Error("missing: <key>")`; it now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` consequently returns a seemingly successful array containing fallback values rather than propagating the missing-data failure.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config fields for current retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers construct the exported Config as { maxAttempts, timeoutMs }. Removing timeoutMs and making retries mandatory makes those consumers fail TypeScript compilation when upgrading, even though retry itself still uses maxAttempts.

findings.title: Surface failure after retryBackground exhausts its attempts
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is exported but catches every thrown failure and returns void once retries are exhausted. Its callers cannot distinguish a successful invocation from an operation that failed on every attempt.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config timeout contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers passing the prior public shape `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check because `retries` and `timeout` are required. JavaScript consumers continue running but `config.timeout` is undefined, so `Date.now() + config.timeout` becomes NaN and the timeout guard never fires.

findings.title: Expose failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: If every invocation of `fn` throws, the new exported function catches every error and then returns `void`, exactly like a successful attempt. Its callers cannot distinguish an exhausted retry failure from success and can proceed as if the background work completed.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing Config consumers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported. Existing callers supplying the previously required { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } can no longer type-check because timeoutMs was removed and retries/timeout are now required; retry also reads only the new timeout property.

findings.title: Make retryBackground actually run in the background
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported retryBackground contract implies work is scheduled away from the caller, but it invokes fn() directly in a synchronous retry loop and can block until the deadline. A caller using it to avoid blocking will instead block on every attempt.

findings.title: Expose exhaustion failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception is discarded and the exported void API returns identically after success, deadline expiry, and retry exhaustion. Callers cannot distinguish a completed background operation from one that never succeeded.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number, but value.length is only meaningful for strings. TypeScript rejects this access, and a numeric value at runtime renders "len=undefined" instead of a valid label.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly permits `number`, but numbers have no `.length`; e.g. `<Field value={42} />` renders an input default value of `len=undefined` instead of a meaningful label.

findings.title: Convert numeric values before measuring length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly accepts number at line 2, but numbers have no length property. A caller passing value={123} receives input text "len=undefined" instead of a valid length label.

findings.title: Preserve capacity for large generated patches
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. The call at line 140 captures the complete git diff as stdout, so a PR whose textual patch exceeds that limit fails before review instead of producing a result. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these patches.

findings.title: Keep the bundle base aligned with the generated patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and changed-file set are both computed from mergeBase (lines 140-141), but the bundle now reports baseSha instead. When the PR target branch has advanced since the head branch diverged, baseSha is not the patch's ancestor; consumers receive base/head metadata that describes a different comparison than the supplied patch.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for Git patch output
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. This helper is used to capture the complete `git diff` patch at line 140, so any review whose patch exceeds 1 MiB now fails before review creation instead of producing a result.

findings.title: Restore sufficient buffer for Git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: `git()` now uses spawnSync's default 1 MiB maxBuffer, but it supplies the complete PR patch at line 140. A PR with a diff exceeding that limit causes `git diff` to fail, so the review aborts before it can post a result.

findings.title: Keep the Codex child read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` launches the agent in `opts.repoPath` without an explicit write denial. A supplied prompt can therefore cause the child agent to modify the repository being reviewed, violating this wrapper's safe review boundary.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` changes `codex exec` from a non-mutating reviewer into an agent allowed to modify the repository at `opts.repoPath`. A review prompt or model/tool-call error can therefore alter, delete, or create repository files while producing a review result.

findings.title: Keep Codex execution read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Without `-s read-only`, Codex runs with its default sandbox instead of the caller-enforced read-only policy. Because this helper sets `cwd` to `opts.repoPath`, a prompt (including untrusted repository content incorporated into one) can cause Codex to create, modify, or delete files in the reviewed repository.

findings.title: Diff against the resolved PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA is supplied, headSha identifies the commit that will receive the review/check, but these calls now compare against HEAD instead. A GitHub Actions checkout can be a synthetic pull-request merge commit, so the generated bundle can include merge/base-side changes that are not in the PR head while the result is posted to PR_HEAD_SHA.

findings.title: Restore the PR merge-base review range
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch tip and that branch has advanced since the PR fork, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes the base-only commits as reverse changes. Those unrelated paths are placed in the review bundle at lines 162-167 and in `changedPaths` for inline-comment eligibility, so Needlefish can review non-PR code and attempt inline comments GitHub does not consider part of the PR.

findings.title: Diff the PR merge base against its declared head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is a newer base-branch commit than the PR's fork point, diffing baseSha..HEAD includes unrelated base-branch commits and files in the review bundle. It also ignores PR_HEAD_SHA when that explicitly selected PR head differs from the checkout, while review comments/checks are still posted to headSha. This produces findings for non-PR changes or reviews a different commit than the one annotated.

findings.title: Preserve dollar sequences in prompt payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $-tokens in a string replacement. A patch containing $& (common in regex replacements) is transformed into the matched placeholder, so the review/critic prompt no longer contains the submitted patch verbatim; $`, $', and $$ are likewise expanded.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences in prompt data
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets $& and related sequences in string replacement values. A submitted patch containing, for example, '+$&' is inserted into critic.md as '+{{PATCH}}' rather than its literal text; bundle or finding content with replacement tokens is likewise altered before Codex reviews it. The reviewer can therefore audit a different patch or context than the actual input.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement specially: `$&` expands to the matched placeholder. Since bundle.patch is arbitrary reviewed source text, a patch containing `$&` is changed to `{{BUNDLE}}` while constructing reviewPrompt, so Codex reviews corrupted input. The same regression affects candidate findings and bundle.patch at lines 32-33 when constructing criticPrompt.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the first review submission fails, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub then attaches the review to the PR's most recent commit, while this run generated its patch and findings from the earlier headSha. If a push occurs during the review, a stale REQUEST_CHANGES verdict is presented as a review of the new, unreviewed head.

findings.title: Keep the review pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the JSON review request fails (for example, due to an invalid inline comment), this fallback now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR is pushed between analysis of headSha and this fallback POST, Needlefish publishes its verdict on the new, unreviewed commit while the accompanying check run remains pinned to the analyzed headSha.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed SHA in the fallback review request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary request fails (the reason this fallback exists), this request now omits commit_id. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, while this run analyzed headSha captured earlier. If the PR is updated before the fallback is sent, a changes-requested or pass review is recorded against code that was never reviewed.

findings.title: Preserve the non-strict parsing contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported API previously accepted `normalizeReview(raw, false)` and omitted every malformed finding. The `strict` argument is now removed and every item is passed to `normalizeFinding`; existing TypeScript callers no longer compile, and JavaScript callers that relied on lenient omission receive fabricated findings (or a TypeError for null entries) instead.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid input is now downgraded into a `Finding` that is indistinguishable from a real one: for example, an invalid severity becomes P1, an invalid category becomes bug, and omitted location and explanation fields become empty/zero values. Consumers can therefore render, report, or act on malformed model output as a real finding rather than receiving the validation failure that this exported function previously propagated.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid review data that previously raised a malformed-finding error is now returned as a seemingly real finding. For example, an invalid severity becomes P1, a missing file becomes an empty path, and a missing line becomes 0, so callers cannot distinguish model/parser failure from an actual P1 finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of synthesizing defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severities/categories and missing required location or explanation fields no longer fail normalization. They become a P1/bug finding with empty strings and zero line numbers, so callers of the exported normalizer cannot distinguish malformed review output from a valid finding and may act on or report fabricated data.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before any actions/checkout step. `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` has neither `-R`, `GH_REPO`, nor a checked-out Git remote from which to determine the repository, so it fails to resolve the PR refs and aborts the manual review workflow.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow_dispatch path has no pull_request payload, so it executes these commands before actions/checkout runs. A PR number alone is not repository-qualified, and without -R (or GH_REPO) gh must infer the repository from a local checkout/default configuration that is not established by this workflow. On a fresh runner it cannot resolve the PR, leaving the manual review path unable to obtain the requested head/base refs.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit for manual PR ref resolution
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and this runs before actions/checkout. Without -R "$REPO", `gh pr view` must infer a repository from the current Git checkout, which is unavailable at this point; head/base outputs are not resolved and the review cannot check out the requested PR.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported normalizer previously rejected malformed or incomplete review payloads. It now replaces missing summary, findings, checked evidence, and residual risks with empty values, so callers cannot distinguish an invalid reviewer response from a valid review that found nothing. That can cause malformed review output to be accepted as a pass-shaped result.

findings.title: Reject malformed review envelopes instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, a missing or wrongly typed summary/findings/checked/residual_risks field raised an error. This change maps each failure to empty data, so a malformed model or transport response is indistinguishable from a valid review with no findings or blocking risks. As normalizeReview is exported, every consumer is forced to treat invalid output as a legitimate result.

findings.title: Restore rejection of malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null, {}, or a payload with a non-array findings field previously raised a malformed-output error; they now return an apparently valid RawReview with empty/default fields. Consumers of this exported function can no longer distinguish an invalid model response from a genuine review with no findings, checked evidence, or residual risks.

findings.title: Resolve PR SHAs for workflow_dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so both expressions evaluate empty. The required pr_number is therefore never resolved to its PR base/head SHA; checkout instead falls back to github.ref (line 29) and the reviewer receives empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA. Manually dispatching this workflow consequently reviews the dispatch ref rather than the requested PR.

score.error: malformed critic output: residual risk was not in the candidate review

findings.title: Restore PR ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch events have no pull_request payload. These expressions therefore expand to empty values, whereas the removed Resolve PR refs step queried the requested pr_number and supplied both SHAs. The same manual path now checks out github.ref and fetches main (lines 29 and 35), neither of which identifies the selected PR, so a manually requested PR can be reviewed against the wrong code/base or invoked without its intended SHA inputs.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default. runLocal reads the complete `git diff` output at line 100, so reviewing a repository change whose patch exceeds 1 MiB now terminates with a buffer-limit error before a review bundle can be created. The previous implementation explicitly supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore a buffer large enough for generated review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal obtains the entire patch through git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at line 100. spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB, so a valid diff exceeding that limit terminates git and this wrapper throws instead of producing a review. The previous implementation explicitly supported up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Keep a buffer large enough for the full git diff
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal obtains the complete patch through git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at src/adapters/local.ts:100. Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync’s 1 MiB default, so a larger PR causes git to terminate with a buffer overflow rather than returning the patch; local review aborts before review() is called.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or posting the review fails, this creates the completed "Needlefish" check with conclusion "neutral". GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check status, so branch protection can allow the PR to merge even though no review completed; the emitted summary explicitly says it did not pass.

findings.title: Keep failed reviews as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review(), posting the review, or posting the normal check throws, this path still states that the PR did not pass but publishes the explicit Needlefish check as neutral. Neutral is accepted by GitHub branch-protection checks, so a required Needlefish check can cease blocking a PR precisely when the reviewer failed to run.

findings.title: Report review execution errors as a failing check
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or result posting throws, the code still says the review did not pass, but publishes the Needlefish check with conclusion "neutral". GitHub treats neutral as successful for required status checks, so a required Needlefish check can allow this PR to merge even though no review completed.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout trusted
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR-head checkout now supplies package scripts, dependencies, and src/cli.ts that run on a self-hosted runner with GH_TOKEN and pull-requests/checks write permissions. A same-repository PR can therefore alter the reviewer to emit a false verdict or execute arbitrary runner commands, defeating the review trust boundary.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the reviewer before installing
findings.whyItBreaks: This repository head contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. The new install command therefore fails before the review step, and the subsequent command cannot locate src/cli.ts.

findings.title: Run Needlefish only from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: A same-repository PR can modify package install hooks, dependencies, or src/cli.ts; this workflow checks out that PR and executes both pnpm install and the modified CLI on a self-hosted runner with a write-capable GitHub token. The prior workflow deliberately used a separate checkout of main to keep the reviewer outside the PR's control.

findings.title: Restore the checkout that contains the review tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out repository at the reviewed head contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install --frozen-lockfile fails, and the subsequent CLI path is nonexistent.

findings.title: Restore a trusted checkout for the reviewer
findings.whyItBreaks: The job checks out the PR head into the workspace, then runs its `pnpm install` and `src/cli.ts`. A same-repository PR can modify either install-time metadata or the CLI to emit a forged review/check or execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner using the supplied `GH_TOKEN` (`pull-requests: write`, `checks: write`). This defeats the review trust boundary.

findings.title: Preserve canonicalization of incoming severities
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw JSON and passes each finding here. A valid severity serialized as "p2" or " P1 " was previously normalized to P2/P1; it now fails the exact-membership check and is emitted as P3, changing the reported priority.

findings.title: Preserve case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview passes untrusted finding objects to normalizeFinding. A valid severity such as " p1 " previously normalized to "P1"; it now fails the exact-membership check and is returned as "P3", silently downgrading the finding.

findings.title: Preserve canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding({ severity: " p2 " } as any) previously returned severity P2, but now falls through to P3 because the value is no longer trimmed and uppercased. normalizeReview accepts untyped JSON, so this silently downgrades valid findings whose severity casing or whitespace differs from the canonical form.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex child
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit sanitized env, spawnSync inherits process.env. runCodex passes its prompt directly to codex exec, so any GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN present in the parent is now available to that agent process and its tool commands. The deleted filtering was the only credential boundary here; read-only sandboxing does not remove inherited secrets.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting `env` makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. `runCodex` passes its caller-supplied prompt directly to an agent that reviews repository-controlled content, so an instruction in that input can cause the subprocess to read or use those credentials. The removed explicit scrubbing was the only protection.

findings.title: Restore GitHub-token scrubbing for the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Without an explicit env object, spawnSync inherits process.env, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. runCodex gives that child the caller-provided prompt and repository working tree; its shell/tool processes can therefore use credentials that the previous implementation deliberately withheld. The read-only sandbox does not make inherited credentials unavailable.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach the self-hosted job, which checks out the fork head and executes `pnpm install` and `tsx src/cli.ts` from that checkout. A fork author can therefore execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository gate for self-hosted execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach this self-hosted job. The workflow explicitly checks out the fork-controlled head SHA, runs dependency installation, and executes fork-controlled TypeScript. A malicious fork can therefore run arbitrary code on the persistent self-hosted runner and access its filesystem, network, or runner credentials.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now reach a self-hosted runner, check out attacker-controlled head code, install its dependencies, and execute its CLI. A fork author can therefore execute arbitrary commands in the runner environment and compromise runner-accessible credentials or infrastructure.

findings.title: Continue accepting zero-valued runner durations
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, setting either runner-delay environment variable to "0" produced a zero-millisecond delay. Now it silently substitutes 5000ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS or 2000ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS. Existing deployments using zero to disable the grace/give-up wait therefore gain an unexpected delay after upgrade.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner grace settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` parsed as zero and made the corresponding timeout stages immediate. This change silently substitutes the 5000 ms and 2000 ms fallbacks, so an existing deployment configured for immediate escalation/return now waits up to seven additional seconds after a runner timeout.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration timeout configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" previously produced a zero-millisecond delay. It now falls back to 5000ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS or 2000ms for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS, so existing deployments that intentionally request immediate SIGKILL escalation or immediate give-up behavior silently wait longer after upgrade.

findings.title: Restore coverage for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapped hotspots are deep-reviewed. The removed tail hotspot was the only path that included changed files omitted by the mapper or excluded by the six-hotspot cap, so a large PR can now receive a clean review while changed files were never inspected.

findings.title: Preserve deep-pass residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep passes can return blocking residual risks, but this replacement always sends an empty array to the critic. The critic and final verdict therefore cannot distinguish an incomplete deep review from one with no risks, allowing a blocking concern to be lost.

findings.title: Restore deep coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews now inspect only the first six mapped hotspots. Any changed file omitted by the mapper, or assigned to a seventh hotspot, receives no deep review and produces no blocking residual risk; the critic is given only patchStat, not that file's diff.

findings.title: Forward deep residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep reviewer can return a blocking residual risk, but this code replaces all such signals with an empty array before constructing the critic input. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a fully reviewed patch from one with unresolved blocking evidence and can return a passing result.

findings.title: Retain coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only the first six mapper hotspots. The removed tail hotspot was the only path that sent changed files omitted by those hotspots to a deep review, so a seventh hotspot or an unmapped changed file is now silently excluded from deep review.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep review can return a blocking residual risk, but this code now replaces all of them with an empty array before invoking the critic. A risk that the deep pass could not resolve therefore never reaches the final verdict path, allowing a non-blocking result where the prior implementation reported a block.

findings.title: Preserve focus and depth controls for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The small-review path still serializes the full Bundle, but the large-review path now removes `focus` and `deep` before constructing the map prompt and no longer substitutes `{{FOCUS}}` into each deep-review prompt. Consequently, a caller requesting a focused or depth-controlled review gets that request ignored exactly when the patch crosses the large-review threshold; the deep prompt may also receive an unresolved `{{FOCUS}}` token.

score.error: malformed critic output: residual risk was not in the candidate review

findings.title: Keep the focus directive in large deep-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted {{FOCUS}} replacement means every large-review deep pass receives the literal placeholder instead of the caller-provided focus. The same request field is also removed from the map payload, so focused large reviews silently behave as unfocused reviews while small reviews still receive the complete bundle.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durationMs=119999, this computes minutes=1 and seconds=60, rendering `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. The same rollover occurs for every minute boundary with a fractional remainder of at least 59.5 seconds.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: At 119500ms, minutes is floored to 1 while remaining seconds rounds to 60, so review output renders "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". At 59500ms it similarly renders "60s" instead of "1m 0s".

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations whose sub-minute remainder rounds to 60 seconds, such as 59,999ms, this returns `60s`; at 119,999ms it returns `1m 60s`. Both should carry into the minute component (`1m 0s` and `2m 0s`), so rendered call and total durations are wrong near every minute boundary.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` return 0 even though both its exported name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. Callers can therefore receive a value outside the documented result domain.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0 even though its exported name and thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. Callers can therefore rely on this validator and receive a non-positive value.

findings.title: Reject zero to preserve the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parsePositiveInteger("0", label) now returns 0, even though its exported name and error contract promise a positive integer. Callers can therefore receive an invalid zero where they rely on this parser to enforce positivity.
